section_1.title: The Hook: Stretching Space
section_1.content: Introduce linear transformation as a stretching/rotating grid. Visualize a 2D plane. Most vectors change direction when a matrix is applied, but some stay on their original span. These are our 'special' vectors.
section_1.example: Visualize a square grid with an image of a cat. Applying a matrix stretches the grid; notice how most cat pixels move to new angles, but pixels along one diagonal line stay locked to that line.

section_2.title: Defining Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
section_2.content: Define the equation Av = λv. The Eigenvector (v) is the direction that remains unchanged. The Eigenvalue (λ) is the scaling factor (how much it stretches or shrinks).
section_2.example: A 'magic wand' arrow (eigenvector) stays pointed at the same spot on the wall even after the room (transformation) expands; its length doubles (eigenvalue = 2).

section_3.title: The Eigenbasis: A New Perspective
section_3.content: Explain that if we have enough independent eigenvectors, they can form a new coordinate system. In this basis, complex matrix multiplication becomes simple diagonal scaling.
section_3.example: A robot arm works in 'X-Y' coordinates (complex), but if we switch to an 'Eigenbasis' of the arm's joints, calculating its reach becomes as simple as adding independent scalar values.

section_4.title: Synthesis & Visual Summary
section_4.content: Summarize the process: 1. Identify the 'locked' directions (eigenvectors), 2. Measure the stretch (eigenvalues), 3. Reframe the system (eigenbasis) to simplify high-dimensional problems.
section_4.example: Showing a complex 'chaos' rotation collapsing into a clean, easy-to-read diagonal matrix once the coordinate system is aligned with the eigenvectors.
